articleSummary: Eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo’s Ituri province is experiencing an Ebola outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus, with at least 80 deaths; 65 deaths and 246 suspected cases were reported last Friday. articleHeadline: Portrait of a killer virus: The virus that refuses to die  --  Ebola's 50-year reign of death
articleSummary: Ebola virus, Zaire strain, remains a lethal threat after five decades, with a fresh outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo killing over 80 and one person in Uganda (as of 2026-05-17). Six strains are known: Zaire, Sudan, Bundibugyo, Reston, Tai Forest, Bombali, with Zaire driving most cases since 2014. Transmission occurs via fruit bats and other animals; human-to-human spread is by direct contact with blood, vomit, or feces, including funeral rites; airborne transmission is not involved. Case fatality ranges 40-70% in DR Congo epidemics. Dormant survivors can relapse years later. Incubation is 2-21 days; early symptoms fever, fatigue, sore throat, then vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, rash, kidney/liver impairment, and possibly bleeding. Vaccines exist for Zaire (Ervebo, Sabdeno); Sudan vaccines have been tested since 2022 with WHO approval; two monoclonal antibodies target Zaire. Rehydration and transfusion remain key. The 2013-2016 West Africa outbreak caused about 11,300 deaths; the August 2025 DR Congo outbreak in Ituri killed at least 34, with containment hampered by movement, gold mining, and armed attacks.

articleSummary: Hantavirus Vaccine Challenges: Transmission is rodent-borne via inhalation of aerosols from urine, feces, or saliva. No specific antiviral treatment or vaccine is approved in the European Union or United States. articleHeadline: WHO declares global health emergency over Ebola outbreak in Congo and Uganda
articleSummary: WHO designates a global health emergency over the Bundibugyo Ebola virus outbreak in Congo and Uganda. The Bundibugyo virus, a rare Ebola variant, has no approved therapeutics or vaccines. As of Saturday, Africa CDC reported 336 suspected cases and 87 deaths, with Congo accounting for all but two cases. Uganda confirmed two cases, one imported from Congo that died in Kampala and a second case also detected in Kampala; the two patients had no clear epidemiological link and both had travelled from Congo. The outbreak began in Congo’s Ituri province, near Uganda and South Sudan. Bundibugyo first emerged during 2007–2008 in Uganda’s Bundibugyo district (149 infections, 37 deaths) and reappeared in 2012 in Isiro, Congo (57 cases, 29 deaths). The WHO noted the outbreak does not meet pandemic criteria and advised against border closures.

The outbreak has killed more than 80 people within the DRC. Authorities warn that there is currently no vaccine available for this particular Ebola strain. The Geneva-based WHO described the event as a 'public health emergency of international concern' but did not elevate the alert to a pandemic emergency, which remains the highest level introduced in 2024.

articleSummary: WHO declares a public health emergency of international concern over Ebola outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (Ituri province) and Uganda, as of May 17, 2026. articleSummary: EBOLA outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (Ituri Province) and Uganda triggers WHO Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC). As of 16 May 2026, Ituri reports 8 lab-confirmed cases, 246 suspected cases, and 80 suspected deaths across Bunia, Rwampara, and Mongbwalu; two lab-confirmed cases (including one death) were reported in Kampala within 24 hours (15–16 May) in individuals from the DRC; a lab-confirmed case was recorded in Kinshasa on 16 May in a traveler from Ituri. WHO Director-General will convene the IBC for temporary recommendations. Advice to countries emphasizes avoiding border closures or travel/trade restrictions; instead, protect travelers, disseminate accurate risk information, and prepare for evacuation of exposed nationals.

articleSummary: As of 17 May 2026, the Democratic Republic of Congo faces a Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak with 80 deaths and at least 246 suspected cases. The World Health Organization declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern but said it does not constitute a pandemic. Eight laboratory-confirmed cases have been reported; suspected cases and deaths are in Bunia (Ituri Province) and the mining towns of Mongvalu and Rvamparu. The Bundibugyo strain has no approved vaccine or specific treatment. Two confirmed cases have been reported in neighboring Uganda; a 59-year-old man who died on Thursday tested positive. WHO recommends emergency operation centers, contact tracing, and isolation/treatment until two Bundibugyo-specific tests, spaced at least 48 hours apart, are negative. Do not close borders; neighboring countries are high risk. Transmission is via direct contact with bodily fluids and broken skin; early symptoms include fever and muscle pains. Ebola was first identified in 1976 in the DRC.

A 10-year-old girl from Dong Thap presented with dengue shock syndrome and progressed to macrophage activation syndrome, a rare hyperinflammatory complication. On admission, hematocrit was 53% and liver enzymes neared 3,000 U/L, with liver and kidney injury and coagulopathy despite fluids. She required respiratory support (NCPAP), albumin, and transfusions. Multidisciplinary teams added dexamethasone to curb inflammation. Within 24 hours fever fell and liver injury stabilized; after a week in ICU she regained consciousness, began eating, and is near discharge. In Ho Chi Minh City, dengue is linked to multi-organ failure and fatalities; more than 16,000 cases this year, up over 70% from 2025. Authorities expect a seasonal rise from mid-June to July and urge vector control, early care for fever, and vaccination for eligible individuals.

articleHeadline: What Is Ebola And Why Has WHO Declared A Global Health Emergency?
articleSummary: Ebola outbreak centered in Congo and Uganda prompts WHO to declare a Global Health Emergency. Communities are urged to avoid direct contact with infected individuals and wildlife, practice hygiene, and report suspected cases quickly. Health workers face high risk without proper PPE; strict infection-control rules and laboratory safety with high-security facilities are essential. Many survivors suffer long-term health problems; the virus can persist in certain body parts for months, and transmission via semen has been documented up to 15 months post-recovery, prompting safer-sex guidance and regular testing for male survivors. Pregnant and breastfeeding women who recover require special medical monitoring. Although current outbreaks are in Congo and neighboring Uganda, the global nature of travel underscores risk of wider spread. The Bundibugyo strain is under study; vaccines and treatments are in development. Early case isolation, contact tracing, and public awareness remain critical.

articleSummary: Bundibugyro virus Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (Ituri province: Bunia, Rwampara, Mongbwalu) was declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern by WHO on 2026-05-17. As of Saturday, 80 suspected deaths, eight laboratory-confirmed cases, and 246 suspected cases have been reported. International spread has occurred: two laboratory-confirmed cases (one death) in Uganda’s capital Kampala among travellers from DRC, and a confirmed case in Kinshasa returning from Ituri. The virus’s natural reservoir includes dense forests in the DRC; transmission requires direct contact with bodily fluids, contaminated materials, or deceased. WHO urges border countries to activate disaster management, implement cross-border and road screening, isolate confirmed cases, monitor contacts daily, and restrict travel for 21 days post-exposure, while advising against blanket border closures to avoid informal crossings.

articleSummary: Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (Ituri) and neighboring Uganda has claimed 88 lives and generated hundreds of suspected cases.
